Champagne, No Hangover: Technical Report

Do champions (and runners-up) fall off more than equally good teams that did not win it all? NFL, NBA, MLB and NHL, every team-season with a usable next season. Companion to the article “Champagne, No Hangover”.

Summary of findings

  • No evidence of a championship hangover beyond regression to the mean, in any league over its full history. Champions fall the next season, but by less than regression to the mean (RTM) predicts in the NFL, NBA and NHL, and by almost exactly what it predicts in MLB (Table 6.2). That is absence of evidence with explicit bounds, not proof of zero (Table 7.4a). The one exploratory exception is modern MLB (Tables 7.7 and 7.8).
  • Against regular-season twins (five nearest non-finalists, own franchise excluded, bias-adjusted, reuse-corrected 95% CIs), champions' next-season change in wins, one-season / two-season match (co-primary): NBA +2.76 [+0.80, +4.72] / +2.57 [+0.61, +4.52]; NHL +2.84 [+1.10, +4.57] / +1.55 [+0.02, +3.07]; NFL +0.99 [+0.11, +1.88] / +0.86 [−0.07, +1.79]; MLB −0.42 [−2.65, +1.82] / −0.70 [−2.87, +1.47]. The NBA and NHL edges exclude zero in both designs (the NHL only barely under two-season matching, lower bound +0.02); the NFL edge is suggestive, not established. MLB point estimates are below zero but small.
  • On the designated primary outcome (change in differential per game; designated in v0.1, not pre-registered), the NHL champion edge excludes zero in both designs (p < 0.001 and 0.018), the NFL's too (p = 0.028, 0.036), the NBA's does not (+0.64 [−0.13, +1.42]). After requiring both designs to agree and Holm-correcting across the 8 primary tests, none survives (smallest adjusted p = 0.144, NHL champions). Pooled across leagues with random effects, the champion edge is +0.18 SD of win% (95% CI +0.08 to +0.28) with one-season matching and +0.15 SD (+0.05 to +0.25) with two-season matching. In wins, 0.18 SD is about 0.6 NFL, 2.2 NBA, 2.5 MLB, 1.7 NHL wins. Heterogeneity is not significant (Q p = 0.317 and 0.302), but with four leagues Q has little power.
  • Why champions beat their twins: most plausibly selection on playoff information, but not established. Champions were chosen by their playoff results, which carry information about quality the regular-season record lacks. When playoff evidence is held equal, estimates land on both sides of zero and are imprecise (Table 7.4). The regressions that hold playoff depth equal remove most of the twin edge; matching on end-of-season Elo does not. On the same champions, the Elo match moves the edge only from +3.04 to +2.36 wins (NBA) and from +1.27 to +1.21 (NFL) (Table 7.6c). Matching each champion to non-finalists that ended the season within 25 Elo points (possible for 27 of 51 NFL and 41 of 69 NBA champions; Elo SMD after matching 0.05 and 0.05) gives NFL +1.21 [−0.43, +2.86] and NBA +2.36 [−0.22, +4.93] wins; these estimates describe the less dominant champions that have an Elo twin, not all champions. v0.2's negative Elo estimates came from a design that left most of the Elo gap in place and extrapolated across it; it is retired (Section 7, Tables 7.4 and 7.6). In the NHL the champion edge given playoff depth is +1.56 wins with rounds entered linearly but +0.81 [−1.79, +3.41] when depth is coded as a share of the rounds available, so part of the "unexplained" NHL title effect was a coding artifact; champion vs runner-up (+1.61 wins, CI includes zero) is the remaining support.
  • Bounds (Table 7.4a). Versus regular-season twins, the data rule out champions falling further than 0.1 NFL wins, show no sign of any extra fall in the NBA and NHL, and cannot exclude a loss of up to 2.9 wins in MLB. For a title-specific hangover (playoff evidence held equal), the weakest design's 95% lower limit is −1.1 wins (NFL, 6.7% of a season), −4.8 (NBA, 5.9%), −6.8 (MLB, 4.2%) and −1.8 (NHL, 2.2%). These are pointwise limits of the least favorable design, not joint bounds. Each is smaller than the league's average RTM drop for champions (NFL 2.9, NBA 6.5, MLB 7.5, NHL 4.4 wins; normal_drop.csv). That comparison is for each league's full history. Since 1980 (exploratory), the bound stays below the era's own RTM drop in the NFL (1.7 vs 2.7) and NHL (2.3 vs 4.1), roughly equals it in the NBA (7.2 vs 7.6), and exceeds it in MLB (14.0 vs 5.9; worst_vs_normal_by_era.csv). In MLB since 1980 the title-only estimates run −8.2 to −3.4 wins; the negative sign holds for splits at 1969, 1980, 1985, 1995 (Table 7.8), but the split was chosen after looking and, across the 24 era-by-design cells, the smallest MLB BH q is 0.060. A lead, not a finding.
  • No Super Bowl loser curse. Losers made the next postseason 69% of the time vs 54% for matched teams. Almost all of the gap is 1970-86 (17 of 17 made it back); since 1987 the rates are close (55% vs 54%).
  • NBA close games: of the NBA champions' +2.76-win edge, +1.10 [+0.16, +2.04] is next-season wins beyond what point differential implies, which is why the NBA edge is clearer in wins than in differential (Section 7).
  • Dose-response: no reliable evidence that longer playoff runs cause bigger drops, but the NHL estimate is imprecise rather than small (Section 9).
  • Repeats: NHL champions repeat more often than regular-season quality predicts, robust to dynasty clustering; the NBA excess is the 1957-69 Celtics (Section 10).

Reading this report

The report explains every step, but it uses some shorthand. One plain-English line per term:

RTM
Regression to the mean: teams picked for an extreme season tend to be closer to average the next season, because part of any extreme season is luck.
Twins / matched controls
For each champion, the five most similar non-finalist teams (same league, within five seasons) on win% and point differential.
ATT
Average gap between each champion and its twins in next-season change ("average treatment effect on the treated"). Positive = champions held up better.
Bias adjustment
A small regression correction for the fact that a champion's twins are usually slightly worse than the champion (Abadie-Imbens).
95% CI
The range of values consistent with the data at the usual 95% level. If it includes zero, the difference could be noise.
Reuse-corrected SE
A standard error that accounts for one twin serving several champions (Abadie-Imbens 2006). Naive errors understate the uncertainty (Table 7.2).
Co-primary designs
One-season matching (title season) and two-season matching (title season and the one before). Claims need both.
p-value
How surprising the estimate would be if the true gap were zero. Below 0.05 = conventionally "significant".
Permutation p
How often shuffling the champion label within its matched set produces a gap this big. Descriptive only in v0.2.
Holm / BH q
Corrections for running many tests: Holm controls the chance of any false positive in the primary family; Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) q controls the share of false positives among all tests.
SMD
Standardized mean difference: the gap between champions and twins on a covariate, in SD units. Below 0.1 is conventionally "balanced".
CR1 / HC1 SEs
Standard errors that allow for correlated errors within a season (CR1) or unequal variances (HC1).
Decade FE
A separate intercept per decade, absorbing league-wide shifts (scoring levels, schedule changes).
Conditional logit
The title-odds model: each season's title is shared out among that season's teams in proportion to exp(quality score), so probabilities sum to 1 per season.
Elo (538)
FiveThirtyEight's team rating, updated after every game including the playoffs; used here as "quality at season's end".
SD units (z)
Win% or differential measured relative to that season's league average, in standard deviations.

What changed in v0.4

v0.4 is the cycle-3 publication check, logged in reports/changelog_c3.md (cycle 2 in changelog_c2.md, cycle 1 in changelog_c1.md). No earlier estimate changed. A new step, 12d_c3_checks.py, adds four checks, and the claims that rest on them are rescoped:

  • Elo coverage. The 25-point Elo match covers 27 of 51 NFL and 41 of 69 NBA champions, the less dominant ones. On exactly those champions the regular-season twin edge is +1.27 (NFL) and +3.04 (NBA) wins, so matching on end-of-season Elo removes little of it (Table 7.6c). The "playoffs are information" reading is therefore described as the most plausible explanation, not an established one.
  • Modern MLB. The exploratory 1980 split now has multiplicity adjustments over all 24 era-by-design cells (Table 7.7) and a split-point check at 1969, 1985 and 1995 (Table 7.8). The negative sign is stable across split points; it does not clear a BH correction for the looks taken.
  • Worst case vs the normal drop, by era. The "bound is smaller than the RTM drop" statement is scoped to each league's full history; since 1980 it fails in MLB and is roughly a tie in the NBA (Table 7.4a).
  • Corrections. "No version of the Elo comparison excludes zero" now says "in wins" (the NFL Elo match does exclude zero on differential, driven by its controls' better regular-season margins); "the same Elo rating" reads "nearly the same"; Table 7.7's empty note cells no longer print "nan"; Table 13 team names are spelled out.

§1Question and hypotheses

The "championship hangover" says title teams underperform the next season because of fatigue (a longer season, a shorter offseason), complacency, distraction or roster erosion. The "Super Bowl loser curse" says the beaten finalist collapses. The competing explanation is regression to the mean: any team selected for being unusually good this season will, on average, be less good next season, champion or not.

  • H1 (hangover beyond RTM): champions' next-season change is worse than that of non-finalist teams with the same regular-season win% and point differential, in the same league and era.
  • H2 (runner-up curse): the same, for the losing finalist.
  • H3 (dose-response): among playoff teams, more playoff games predict a larger next-season drop, holding regular-season quality fixed.

What H1 can and cannot show. Champions are selected on playoff success, which is extra evidence of quality. Conditional on the regular season, a champion is therefore expected to be better next season than its twins even with no hangover. The H1 estimate is (quality signal) + (hangover, if any): a positive estimate cannot rule out a hangover. Section 7 (Table 7.4) therefore adds designs that hold playoff evidence equal and reports what each design can rule out.

Outcomes: next-season change in win% (reported in wins per current-length season: NFL 17, NBA 82, MLB 162, NHL 82 games), change in point/run/goal differential per game (the designated primary outcome, chosen in v0.1 because it is less noisy than win%; there is no pre-registration), next-season playoff qualification, and next-season title. Wins are shown throughout for readability, and the report says where the two outcomes disagree.

What would change our mind: a significantly negative champion effect against teams that were equally good after the playoffs (Elo-matched, runner-up, M2/M3 with either depth coding), or a consistently negative effect across the robustness grid in any league. The closest the study comes is modern MLB (Tables 7.7 and 7.8, exploratory).

§2Data sources

All sources are free and machine-readable, downloaded or copied by 01_download_raw.py, which records every file, URL, size and retrieval time in data/raw/manifest.csv (167 files; MLB 15.6 MB, NBA 21.6 MB, NFL 3.4 MB, NHL 2.3 MB). Season labels: NBA and NHL seasons are labelled by the year they end (NBA 2025 = 2024-25). NFL and MLB seasons are labelled by the year they are played; for the NFL that is the year the season starts (the 2024 season ended with Super Bowl LIX in February 2025). §3Cleaning, validation and sample counts

Each league is reduced to one row per team-season with the same columns (_common.SCHEMA): games, wins, losses, ties, points for/against, playoff games, playoff wins/losses, playoff rounds (series) won, champion and runner-up flags. v0.2 adds playoff points for/against (NFL, NBA, NHL), NFL rounds survived (a bye counts as a round) and end-of-season Elo (NFL 1970-2020, NBA 1947-2015). Team identity is the franchise (relocations keep their history).

Cleaning rules

  • NBA: 538 "Tiebreaker" games (1948-1957, flagged as playoffs) dropped; ESPN All-Star/exhibition rows dropped; NBA Cup championship games (which do not count in the standings) dropped; play-in games are neither regular season nor playoffs.
  • NHL: win% = (W + 0.5×T)/GP; overtime and shootout losses count as losses. Goals for and against are the stats API totals, which leave out shootout-deciding goals (official standings credit a shootout win as one goal for, a shootout loss as one against). The difference is a few goals a season (2022-23 Devils: 289-222 in the data, 291-226 official). Records quoted for readers use the official W-L-OTL form and official goal totals (e.g. 2022-23 Devils 52-22-8, 291-226). Playoff ties (1927-1951) are no longer counted as playoff losses. The 2020 qualifying round-robin games remain counted as playoff games.
  • NFL: rounds survived = rounds before a team's first playoff game (byes) + playoff wins; rounds are the season's distinct playoff weekends.
  • All leagues: win% and differential are per-game rates, so strike, lockout, war and pandemic seasons are on the same scale. They are not equally reliable: a 60-game record is a noisier signal than a 162-game one and regresses harder. v0.2 flags interrupted seasons (NFL 1982, 1987; MLB 1918, 1919, 1981, 1994, 1995, 2020; NBA 1999, 2012, 2020, 2021; NHL 1995, 2013, 2020, 2021) and matches exactly on whether this season and next season were shortened. The robustness grid (Section 11) also drops them.
  • MLB 1904 and 1994 had no World Series: for 1903 and 1993 team-seasons, next-season playoff and title outcomes are set to missing (v0.1 treated them as 0).
  • Cross-source mapping (ESPN id to 538 franchise, Stats API id to Lahman franchise, nflverse to 538 codes) is done automatically by matching overlapping games or season lines.

§4Method, step by step

4.1 Definitions

wp = (W + 0.5·T) / GP diff_pg = (PF − PA) / GP (points, runs or goals per game) wp_z = (wp − mean_season(wp)) / sd_season(wp) (standardized within league-season) d_wp = wp(next season) − wp(this season); d_diff likewise wins = d_wp × G_league, G = 17 (NFL), 82 (NBA), 162 (MLB), 82 (NHL)

4.2 Regression-to-the-mean benchmark (08_rtm_models.py)

For each league, fit on non-finalist team-seasons only (so champions cannot shape their own benchmark):

y_next = a + b1·wp + b2·diff_pg + Σ d_k·1[decade = k] + e, y ∈ {wp, diff_pg}

For a champion, expected next = fitted value; excess = actual next − expected next. The 95% CI comes from a season-cluster bootstrap (resample whole seasons, refit, recompute; B = 2,000). Indicator models on all team-seasons, CR1 SEs clustered by season:

M1: y_next = a + b1·wp + b2·diff_pg + g1·champion + g2·runner_up + decade FE M2: M1 + g3·made_playoffs + g4·rounds_survived M3: M2 + g5·playoff_win% + g6·playoff_diff_per_game (MLB: playoff win% only; no playoff run data)

4.3 Matching (09_matched_analysis.py)

For each champion i, candidate controls are teams in the same league, within ±5 seasons, that were not a finalist that season, have a next season, are not i's own franchise, and have the same shortened-season pattern (this season, next season). Distance, with SDs per league over complete seasons:

one-season: dist(i, j) = sqrt( ((wp_j − wp_i)/SD_wp)² + ((diff_j − diff_i)/SD_diff)² ) two-season: the same over (wp, diff_pg, prev_wp, prev_diff), prev = previous PLAYED season

The k = 5 nearest are the matched set M(i) (with replacement across champions, no caliper). Because champions sit at the top of the distribution, their nearest neighbours are still slightly worse on average (Table 7.3), and better teams regress more, so the estimator is bias-adjusted:

Y~_j = Y_j + b'(X_i − X_j), b from OLS of Y on (1, X) over the distinct matched controls ATT = (1/N) Σ_i [ Y_i − (1/k) Σ_{j∈M(i)} Y~_j ] = (1/N) Σ_i d_i

Inference (v0.2). Controls are reused: one control can serve several champions, so the d_i are not independent. The Abadie-Imbens (2006) variance accounts for this. With K_j = Σ_{i: j∈M(i)} 1/k_i the total weight on control j:

V = (1/N²) [ N/(N−1)·Σ_i (d_i − ATT)² + Σ_j σ²_j ( K_j² − Σ_{i: j∈M(i)} 1/k_i² ) ] σ²_j = (Y_j − Y_l(j))² / 2, l(j) = nearest other non-finalist to j (same league, window, short-season pattern) 95% CI = ATT ± 1.96·sqrt(V); p two-sided normal

The first term is the naive variance (v0.1's bootstrap); the second is the extra variance from reuse. The SE still ignores uncertainty in b, so it remains slightly optimistic. The within-set permutation p (v0.1's second test) holds b fixed and ignores reuse; it is reported as descriptive only.

Multiplicity. 4 leagues × 2 groups × 4 outcomes × 2 designs = 64 tests, all with BH q-values. Primary family = change in differential, champion and runner-up in 4 leagues (8 cells). A cell counts only if both co-primary designs agree: p_IUT = max(p_one-season, p_two-season) (intersection-union test), then Holm across the 8.

4.4 Holding playoff evidence equal (12b_playoff_quality.py)

Three designs compare champions with teams that were equally good after the playoffs: (a) M2/M3 above, plus M2s/M3s, which code playoff depth as rounds survived divided by the most rounds any team survived that season (formats had 2, 3 or 4 rounds; 08b_depth_share.py); (b) champion vs the runner-up it beat (same season, regression-adjusted for any regular-season gap, bootstrap over seasons); (c) NFL 1970-2020 and NBA 1947-2015: matching on FiveThirtyEight Elo after each team's last game, playoffs included. v0.3's main Elo design keeps up to five non-finalists within 25 Elo points (same pool rules as 4.3) and drops champions with none, so it covers the champions that have an Elo twin, not the most dominant ones. It is bias-adjusted on Elo; a variant adjusts on Elo, wp and differential. The 538 NFL update rule (K = 20, margin-of-victory multiplier) was reproduced from the pre-game ratings to within 0.01 Elo points for every game.

M2s: y_next = a + b1·wp + b2·diff_pg + g1·champion + g2·runner_up + g3·made_playoffs + g4·(rounds_survived / max rounds that season) + decade FE

MLB caveat: before 1969 the World Series was the only round, so rounds survived equals the champion dummy and the MLB champion coefficient in M2 and M2s is identified from 1969 on only.

4.5 Dose-response (10_dose_response.py)

A1: d_y = a + b·po_gp + c1·wp + c2·diff_pg + decade FE (all playoff teams) A2: A1 + fixed effects for playoff rounds survived (same depth, more games) B : excess_y = a + b·extra_games + decade FE (champions only)

For a champion, extra games beyond the minimum = playoff losses. NFL champions never lose a playoff game, so their dose is games played (3 with a bye, 4 without).

4.6 Repeat rates (11_repeat_simulation.py)

P(team i wins | season s) = exp(b1·wp_z_i + b2·diff_z_i) / Σ_{j in s} exp(b1·wp_z_j + b2·diff_z_j) (conditional logit)

Benchmarks: lottery (1/n_teams); quality only (every title-season team's next-season wp_z and diff_z drawn from the z-scale RTM model plus a resampled residual pair, 2,000 draws; the champion's share of the next-season field); given next-season quality (the model at every team's actual next-season numbers). Inference: 100,000 simulated sums of independent Bernoullis, and a dynasty-robust block bootstrap (a franchise's titles no more than two seasons apart form one block).

§5Worked example: the Oklahoma City Thunder, 2024-25

One champion, end to end, with the numbers the scripts produce (14_cases_worked_example.py → worked_example.csv, worked_example_controls.csv).

Step 1: raw numbers

title season: 68-14, wp = 68/82 = 0.8293 PF 9881, PA 8826 → diff_pg = (9881 − 8826) / 82 = +12.866 playoffs: 23 games = 16 wins + 7 losses → extra games beyond the minimum = 7 next season: 64-18, wp = 0.7805, diff_pg = +11.146 d_wp = 0.7805 − 0.8293 = −0.0488 → × 82 = −4.00 wins

Step 2: what regression to the mean predicts

The NBA base model, fitted on 1,520 non-finalist team-seasons, gives (the last term is the 2020s decade intercept, a small bump absorbing league-wide shifts in that decade):

expected next wp = 0.4115 + 0.1257×wp + 0.0164×diff_pg + 0.0265 = 0.4115 + 0.1257×0.8293 + 0.0164×12.866 + 0.0265 = 0.7531 expected change = (0.7531 − 0.8293) × 82 = −6.24 wins excess = actual − expected = −4.00 − (−6.24) = +2.24 wins

Most of the weight sits on differential: a +12.9 differential team is expected to lose several games of win% next season simply because some of that margin was luck and some of the roster will not be as good. The 7 extra playoff games enter the dose-response analysis in Section 9.

Step 3: the five matched controls

Distance uses the league SDs (wp 0.1502, diff 4.607). The bias-adjustment slopes, fitted over all 209 distinct NBA champion controls, are b_wp = −0.8867 and b_diff = 0.0160. Table 5.1 lists each control's raw change and its adjusted change.

adjustment_j = −0.8867×(wp_i − wp_j) + 0.0160×(diff_i − diff_j) mean control d_wp (raw) = −0.0878 mean control d_wp (adjusted) = −0.0892 champion − controls = −0.0488 − (−0.0892) = +0.0404 → +3.31 wins

This one champion's gap (+3.31 wins) is larger than its RTM excess (+2.24) because five twins is a small sample: these five fell 7.2 wins on average (the 2022 Phoenix Suns alone dropped 19), more than the model's 6.2. It enters the NBA average in Table 7.1 with weight 1/79.

§6Regression to the mean is the main event

Before asking about champions, it helps to see how strongly any team regresses. Table 6.1 gives the base-model coefficients (non-finalists). Units matter when reading them: b_wp is per unit of win% and b_diff per point of differential, so in the NBA +0.100 of win% this season adds +0.0126 next season while +1 point per game of differential adds +0.0164. Differential carries most of the signal once both are in, the familiar result that close-game luck does not persist.

The indicator regressions (Table 6.3) add the playoff dimension. In M1 the champion coefficient is positive in the NFL, NBA and NHL. M2 adds playoff qualification and rounds survived; M3 adds playoff win% and margin. With playoff evidence in the model, the champion coefficient on next-season win% is NFL +0.60 wins [−0.75, +1.95], NBA −0.72 wins [−3.84, +2.40], MLB +0.50 wins [−2.23, +3.23], NHL +1.56 wins [−0.69, +3.81] (M2). These CIs are wide: M2 cannot distinguish "the title adds nothing beyond playoff depth" from a title effect of a few wins in either direction. The pattern differs by league. In the NBA the point estimates turn negative and rounds survived carries the signal (+1.46 wins per round, p = 0.001), which fits the "playoffs are information" reading. In the NHL rounds survived adds almost nothing (+0.25 wins per round, p = 0.423) and the champion coefficient keeps most of its M1 size; on differential it stays significant (p = 0.045). That NHL reading depends on how depth is coded. Rounds survived enters M2 linearly, but NHL formats had two rounds in 34 seasons, three in 19 and four in 45, so the champion dummy partly absorbs "survived every round the format had". Coded as a share of the rounds available (Table 6.4), the NHL champion coefficient falls to +0.81 wins [−1.79, +3.41], about half. Part of the NHL title effect is a coding artifact; champion vs runner-up (Table 8.2) is the remaining evidence for it, and this report does not have an explanation for what is left.

Reading Table 7.1: the NBA and NHL champion win edges exclude zero in both designs, the NHL's only barely in the two-season design (lower bound +0.02). The NHL edge also excludes zero on differential in both designs. The NFL edge excludes zero in the one-season design only, so it is suggestive. The NBA edge appears in wins but not differential: NBA champions win more games than their twins without a clear margin advantage. A direct check (close_game_check.csv) confirms it: measuring each season's wins beyond what point differential implies, champions' next seasons run +1.10 wins [+0.16, +2.04] ahead of their twins', about 40% of the +2.76-win edge. MLB is null in both designs, with point estimates below zero.

Because the regular-season twin comparison bundles the playoff quality signal with any hangover, Table 7.4 lists every design side by side, grouped by what it holds equal, in wins and as a share of a season (the lower 95% limit). Read the "title only" rows for the hangover question: they compare champions with teams that went as deep, played as well in the playoffs, lost the final, or ended the season with nearly the same Elo rating (within 25 points).

The Elo design (rebuilt in v0.3). Champions end the season 100 (NFL) and 78 (NBA) Elo points above their one-season regular-season twins (SMD 0.86, 0.64), because their last games are playoff wins. v0.2's design (E2: Elo, wp and differential, no caliper) closed only about a third of that gap (65 and 55 points left, SMD 0.56 and 0.45), and its estimates (−0.67, −0.66 wins) came from the linear adjustment extrapolating across the rest: unadjusted they are +0.15 and −0.04, and with adjustment slopes fitted on all non-finalists −0.14 and −0.17. v0.3 matches on Elo within 25 points instead. That is feasible for 27 of 51 NFL and 41 of 69 NBA champions (the most dominant have no non-finalist within 25 points), leaves a mean gap of 5.5 and 5.9 points (SMD 0.05, 0.05), and gives +1.21 [−0.43, +2.86] (NFL) and +2.36 [−0.22, +4.93] (NBA) wins; unadjusted +1.23 and +2.30. NFL Elo twins had better regular seasons than the champions (differential SMD −0.58); adjusting for that as well gives +0.62. Once it actually matches on Elo, the comparison is centered at or above zero, and no version of it excludes zero in wins. On differential, the NFL Ec estimate does (+4.96 points a game [+1.66, +8.27]), but that reflects the Elo twins' better regular-season margins; adjusting for them gives +1.14 [−1.68, +3.96]. E2 is kept in Tables 7.4 and 7.6 for disclosure but not used in the bound; had it been kept, the NFL title-only bound would be −1.65.

Table 7.4a condenses it. "Bound vs twins" is the lowest 95% limit across the two co-primary designs. "Bound, title only" is the lowest limit across the title-only designs: the largest title-specific hangover the least favorable design cannot exclude. It is a pointwise limit of the weakest design, not a joint bound, so it is conservative. The title-only designs that hold playoff depth equal also net out any fatigue shared by all deep runs; fatigue is examined separately in Section 9, where the estimate is imprecise rather than small. The next column is the league's average RTM drop for champions (normal_drop.csv): over each league's full history the title-only bound is smaller than the drop regression to the mean already predicts, in MLB only just (6.75 vs 7.49). The last two columns repeat the comparison since 1980 (exploratory, worst_vs_normal_by_era.csv). With half the sample the bounds widen: the NFL and NHL bounds stay well below the era's RTM drop, the NBA's roughly equals it, and the MLB bound is 2.4 times it. The "smaller than the normal drop" statement is a full-history statement and does not hold for modern MLB.

Coverage (v0.4). The Ec estimand is the champions that have an Elo twin: mean end-of-season Elo 1707 (NFL) and 1655 (NBA), against 1771 and 1742 for the champions it drops. Its estimate is therefore not comparable with the all-champion twin edge. Table 7.6c re-estimates the one-season twin design on exactly the covered champions (elo_coverage_check.csv). On the same teams, matching on Elo instead of the regular season moves the NFL edge from +1.27 to +1.21 wins and the NBA edge from +3.04 to +2.36. End-of-season Elo, which includes the playoff games, explains little of the edge for these champions. Either Elo's modest playoff updates (K = 20 per game) understate what a title run reveals, or part of the edge is not playoff information. The regression designs, which hold rounds survived equal, remove most of the NBA edge and roughly half or more of the NFL and NHL edges. The designs disagree, and this report treats "the playoffs are information" as the most plausible explanation, not an established one.

Modern MLB is the one place where the title-only designs lean toward a drop: M2 (rounds, linear) −6.8, M2s (share of rounds) −8.2, champion vs runner-up −3.4 wins, two of three with CIs excluding zero. The split was chosen after looking, and it was run in 24 cells (4 leagues, 2 eras, 3 designs). Adjusted over those 24, the two MLB regression cells have Holm p 0.151 and BH q 0.060: suggestive, not significant. The only cell that survives Holm is positive (NBA champion vs runner-up before 1980, +7.0 wins).

Table 7.8 asks whether 1980 is a lucky cut. It re-runs the three MLB title-only designs on the seasons from 1969 (league championship series), 1985 (seven-game LCS) and 1995 (wild card) onward (mlb_split_sensitivity.csv). Every estimate is negative, and from 1985 on the champion vs runner-up comparison, which uses no depth model, also excludes zero. The slices are nested and small (30 to 55 champions), so this is one lead seen from several angles rather than independent confirmation. The matched post-1980 MLB estimate against regular-season twins is −0.14. Modern World Series winners are not worse than their regular-season twins; they are worse than the teams they beat or that went as deep. This is not evidence of a hangover, but it is the study's strongest lead, and the full-period MLB bound understates how uncertain the modern era is.

§8Runners-up and the Super Bowl loser curse

Runners-up match their peers on wins in every league and both designs (Table 7.1). For the NFL, 17 of 55 Super Bowl losers since 1970 missed the next postseason. That is not a curse: matched teams of the same quality made the playoffs at an adjusted rate of 54%, so they missed 46% of the time, more often than Super Bowl losers (31%). Table 8.1 splits this by era (the Writer's question R-1): almost all of the gap is 1970-86, when every loser made it back; since 1987 losers and their twins are close (a +1.6-point difference).

No specification shows a runner-up decline. The MLB runner-up group did rise unusually into the pennant season (Table 11.4), and its next season is still null.

§9Dose-response: longer runs, shorter offseasons

If fatigue or a short offseason drives a hangover, teams that played more playoff games should fall more. Table 9.1 uses every playoff team. A1 is confounded in a known direction (going deeper is itself evidence of quality), and indeed its slopes are positive or flat. A2 compares teams that survived the same number of rounds, so extra games mean longer series.

§10How often should a champion repeat?

If titles were driven by regular-season quality alone, how many repeats should we see? Table 10.1 compares actual repeats with three benchmarks, each with two p-values: independent Bernoullis (as in v0.1) and a dynasty-robust block bootstrap. MLB 1903 and 1993 champions are excluded (no World Series the next year).

Reading it: NBA and NHL champion win edges exclude zero in nearly every adjusted specification; the NBA differential edge rarely does. The NFL champion edge excludes zero in about half. MLB champions never exclude zero when adjusted; unadjusted, 2 specifications exclude zero below zero (two-season (co-primary): −2.58 [−4.81, −0.35]; k=10: −2.45 [−4.65, −0.25]). Unadjusted matching is biased toward a drop (Table 7.3), and the adjusted versions of the same specifications are near zero, but these are the only estimates anywhere in the study that point to a hangover and they are reported rather than hidden. The caliper specification (champions without a close twin dropped) gives MLB −1.14 wins, more negative than the primary.

Balance placebo: the season before

If one-season matching produced comparable teams, finalists and their twins should have risen equally into the matched season. v0.1 presented a difference here as supporting evidence; it is a failed balance test. Under one-season matching the difference excludes zero for NFL champions (−0.98), NBA champions (−3.38), NHL champions (−2.82), NHL runners-up (−1.57). The MLB runner-up group rose +2.00 wins more than its twins (unadjusted +3.04, p = 0.007), the one group that spiked into its final. This imbalance is why two-season matching is co-primary. The two-season rows of Table 11.4 are a balance check, not a placebo: the two-season design matches on the previous season, so the rise into the matched season is balanced by construction. After it, only one group, MLB runners-up (+2.39) still shows a pre-trend difference excluding zero. The conclusions that survive both designs are the NBA and NHL win edges (the NHL's barely), the NHL differential edge, and the MLB null.

The genuine placebo for the two-season design is the change from two seasons before to the season before (t−2 to t−1), which it does not match on. Table 11.4b gives it, unadjusted and adjusted. All eight unadjusted CIs include zero; adjusted, one of eight just excludes it (NHL champions, −1.79 wins, p = 0.048): NHL champions' twins had risen a little faster two seasons back, a small caution on the NHL two-season edge.

Pooled across leagues

Matching on within-season z-scores in each league, with the same bias adjustment and reuse-corrected SEs, and pooling by inverse variance gives a single estimate on a common scale. Table 11.5 gives fixed- and random-effects (DerSimonian-Laird) pooled estimates and the heterogeneity tests; Table 11.6 the per-league inputs. In v0.1 the pool used unadjusted matching and showed significant heterogeneity; with the v0.2 design the four leagues are consistent (champions: Q p = 0.317 on win%). With only four leagues, Q has little power to detect real differences, so "consistent" means "no evidence of inconsistency". Table 11.5b gives the same pool for the two-season design, and Table 11.5c translates both into wins per league (within-season SD of win% × games): the same 0.18 SD is 0.6 wins in the NFL, 2.2 wins in the NBA, 2.5 wins in the MLB, 1.7 wins in the NHL.

§12Mechanism check: MLB roster age and retention

Lahman player files allow roster measures for MLB through 2021 (13_mlb_roster.py): playing-time-weighted age, and retention: the share of the title season's playing time (PA + batters faced) produced by players who appear for the club the next season. Retention is measured ex ante. v0.1 used continuity (share of next season's playing time going to returners), which rises when returners stay healthy and play well, so it is partly the outcome; it is shown for reference only. Table 12.1 compares finalists with their one-season matched controls.

Table 12.1 MLB roster measures vs matched controls

GroupMeasurenTreatedControlsDifference95% CIp
championroster_age11728.57728.614−0.035[−0.225, +0.155]0.721
championretention1160.8460.795+0.051[+0.037, +0.064]<0.001
championcontinuity_next1160.8200.781+0.040[+0.022, +0.056]<0.001
runner-uproster_age11728.58328.649−0.071[−0.302, +0.150]0.532

Champions were not older than equally good teams (difference −0.03 years) and kept more of their roster (84.6% of title-season playing time returned vs 79.5%). Across all MLB teams, roster age does predict decline: each extra year of weighted age is worth −0.66 wins next season (95% CI −1.00 to −0.32, n = 2,554), but that is not a champion-specific mechanism. Retention is consistent with champions holding up, not proof of why: clubs may keep players precisely because they expect to stay good.

§13Famous cases (from the data)

Table 13.1 lists the three worst next seasons relative to the RTM expectation in each league. Several are well-known breakups or retirements rather than tired champions (the 1997 Marlins' sell-off, the 1998 Bulls' breakup, John Elway's retirement after the 1998 season, Bill Russell's after 1969). Not all are hangovers in any sense: the 1948 Toronto Maple Leafs fell 8.0 wins short of expectation and still won the title again, a reminder that a regular-season shortfall is not a hangover.

§14Limitations

  • Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. The study finds no hangover; Table 7.4 states how large a hangover it cannot exclude. For a title-specific effect those bounds are about one to seven wins (2 to 7% of a season, the weakest design's pointwise limit), which is not small, though over each league's full history each is smaller than the drop regression to the mean predicts. Since 1980 that comparison fails in MLB and is roughly a tie in the NBA (Table 7.4a). Modern MLB is the study's strongest lead toward a title-specific cost (Tables 7.7 and 7.8), found after looking and not significant after correction.
  • Selection on playoff success. The positive champion edge vs regular-season twins is most plausibly read as champions being better than their regular-season line, but that is not established. Designs that hold playoff evidence equal are imprecise, sensitive to how playoff depth is coded, and disagree: the depth regressions remove most of the edge, the Elo match removes little of it on the same champions (Table 7.6c). Part of the NHL edge that survived them in v0.2 was a coding artifact, and what is left is unexplained. The Elo design covers only champions with an Elo twin (about 57% of NFL and NBA champions, the less dominant ones).
  • Small samples per league. 352 champions in total; per-league CIs are wide, and nothing in the primary family survives Holm correction once both designs must agree.
  • Matching imperfection. The best champions (e.g. 72-10, 73-9 NBA teams) have no equally good non-finalist peers; bias adjustment relies on linearity; the reuse-corrected SE ignores uncertainty in the adjustment slope.
  • Outcome choice. Differential per game was designated primary in v0.1 without pre-registration (no timestamped plan exists). Wins and differential disagree in the NBA; both are reported everywhere.
  • Era structure. Matching within ±5 seasons on raw win% mixes rule regimes (NHL ties vs shootouts; NFL playoff-field changes in 1978, 1990, 2020). The z-score specification addresses scale shifts, not every structural change. MLB "made the playoffs" before 1969 means "won the pennant".
  • Dose is a proxy. Playoff games stand in for fatigue and offseason length; offseason days, injuries and minutes are not observed. NHL 2020 round-robin games still count as playoff games.
  • Mechanism data are thin. Roster retention and age are MLB-only and end in 2021; no payroll or cap data.
  • Minor data gaps. A handful of ESPN NBA games are missing in 2017-2018; NBA rounds won in the 1950s round-robin years are approximate; early NBA byes are not coded as rounds survived.

§15Reproducibility

Run the scripts in numeric order (08b after 08; 12b, 12c and 12d after 12) from scripts/ with Python 3.12, pandas 3, numpy, scipy, matplotlib, pyarrow, openpyxl, requests, lxml and bs4 (no statsmodels or scikit-learn: OLS, cluster-robust SEs, the Abadie-Imbens variance, IRLS and conditional logit, bootstraps and permutation tests are implemented in _common.py and the scripts). Random seed 20260923. Step 08's season bootstrap is the slow step (about 8 to 15 minutes on an 8 GB laptop). Table 15.1 maps scripts to outputs.
